claim: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) detect microbial infections and trigger innate immune responses.
source: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) detect microbial infections and trigger innate immune responses.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TLR function.

claim: TLR13 detects the 23S ribosomal RNA of both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
source: Here we show that TLR13 detects the 23S ribosomal RNA of both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: A sequence containing 13 nucleotides near the active site of 23S rRNA ribozyme is both necessary and sufficient to trigger TLR13-dependent interleukin-1β production.
source: A sequence containing 13 nucleotides near the active site of 23S rRNA ribozyme, which catalyzes peptide bond synthesis, was both necessary and sufficient to trigger TLR13-dependent interleukin-1β production.
evidence: This claim is supported by deletion analysis and synthetic RNA experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The 23S rRNA ribozyme catalyzes peptide bond synthesis.
source: A sequence containing 13 nucleotides near the active site of 23S rRNA ribozyme, which catalyzes peptide bond synthesis, was both necessary and sufficient to trigger TLR13-dependent interleukin-1β production.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ribosome function.

claim: Single point mutations within the 13-nucleotide sequence destroyed the ability of the 23S rRNA to stimulate the TLR13 pathway.
source: Single point mutations within this sequence destroyed the ability of the 23S rRNA to stimulate the TLR13 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Knockout of TLR13 in mice abolished the induction of interleukin-1β and other cytokines by the 23S rRNA sequence.
source: Knockout of TLR13 in mice abolished the induction of interleukin-1β and other cytokines by the 23S rRNA sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using TLR13 knockout mice shown in Figure 6.

claim: TLR13 detects bacterial RNA with exquisite sequence specificity.
source: Thus, TLR13 detects bacterial RNA with exquisite sequence specificity.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the point mutation experiments and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: All TLRs contain extracellular leucine-rich repeats (LRRs) and an intracellular Toll-interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain.
source: All TLRs contain extracellular leucine-rich repeats (LRRs) and an intracellular Toll-interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain that recruits MyD88 and other adaptor proteins to activate signal transduction cascades, which culminate in the production of inflammatory cytokines and other antimicrobial molecules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR structure.

claim: The TIR domain recruits MyD88 and other adaptor proteins to activate signal transduction cascades.
source: All TLRs contain extracellular leucine-rich repeats (LRRs) and an intracellular Toll-interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain that recruits MyD88 and other adaptor proteins to activate signal transduction cascades, which culminate in the production of inflammatory cytokines and other antimicrobial molecules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR signaling.

claim: TLR signaling cascades culminate in the production of inflammatory cytokines and other antimicrobial molecules.
source: All TLRs contain extracellular leucine-rich repeats (LRRs) and an intracellular Toll-interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain that recruits MyD88 and other adaptor proteins to activate signal transduction cascades, which culminate in the production of inflammatory cytokines and other antimicrobial molecules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR function.

claim: Vertebrate TLRs comprise 6 major families: TLR1, TLR3, TLR4, TLR5, TLR7 and TLR11.
source: Vertebrate TLRs comprise 6 major families, TLR1, TLR3, TLR4, TLR5, TLR7 and TLR11 (Roach et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roach et al., 2005.

claim: The TLR1 family includes TLR1, TLR2, TLR6, TLR10 and TLR14.
source: The TLR1 family includes TLR1, TLR2, TLR6, TLR10 and TLR14, which are localized on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR classification.

claim: TLR1 family members are localized on the plasma membrane.
source: The TLR1 family includes TLR1, TLR2, TLR6, TLR10 and TLR14, which are localized on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR localization.

claim: TLR2 forms a heterodimer with other members of the TLR1 family (e.g., TLR1, TLR6 or TLR10) to detect microbial lipopeptides and peptidoglycans.
source: Within this family, TLR2 forms a heterodimer with other member of the family (e.g., TLR1, TLR6 or TLR10) to detect microbial lipopeptides and peptidoglycans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR2 function.

claim: TLR4 resides on the plasma membrane and detects bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
source: TLR4 and TLR5 also reside on the plasma membrane and detect bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and flagellin, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR4 function.

claim: TLR5 resides on the plasma membrane and detects flagellin.
source: TLR4 and TLR5 also reside on the plasma membrane and detect bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and flagellin, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR5 function.

claim: TLR4, after binding to LPS, can traffic to endosomal membrane where it launches a signaling cascade leading to the production of type-I interferons (IFNα and IFNβ).
source: TLR4, after binding to LPS, can also traffic to endosomal membrane where it launches a signaling cascade leading to the production of type-I interferons (IFNα and IFNβ).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR4 signaling.

claim: Members of the TLR3, TLR7 and TLR11 families are localized on the endosomal membrane.
source: Members of the remaining TLR families, TLR3, TLR7 and TLR11 are localized on the endosomal membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR localization.

claim: TLR3 detects double-stranded RNA and induces inflammatory cytokines and interferons.
source: TLR3 detects double-stranded RNA and induces inflammatory cytokines and interferons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR3 function.

claim: The TLR7 subfamily consists of TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9.
source: The TLR7 subfamily consists of TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR classification.

claim: TLR7 and TLR8 detect single-stranded RNA.
source: TLR7 and TLR8 detect single-stranded RNA whereas TLR9 binds unmethylated CpG DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR7 and TLR8 function.

claim: TLR9 binds unmethylated CpG DNA.
source: TLR7 and TLR8 detect single-stranded RNA whereas TLR9 binds unmethylated CpG DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR9 function.

claim: The TLR11 family consists of TLR11-13 in mice and TLR21-23 in fish and frogs.
source: The TLR11 family consists of TLR11-13 in mice and TLR21-23 in fish and frogs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR classification.

claim: TLR11 recognizes a profilin-like protein from the parasite Toxoplasma gondii.
source: TLR11 has been shown to recognize a profilin-like protein from the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and an unknown ligand from uropathogenic E. coli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR11 function.

claim: TLR11 recognizes an unknown ligand from uropathogenic E. coli.
source: TLR11 has been shown to recognize a profilin-like protein from the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and an unknown ligand from uropathogenic E. coli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR11 function.

claim: The ligands and roles of TLR12 and TLR13 were unknown prior to this study.
source: The ligands and roles of TLR12 and TLR13 are unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: 10 TLRs (TLR1–10) have been identified in humans.
source: To date, 10 TLRs (TLR1–10) have been identified in humans and 12 (TLR1–9, TLR11–13) in mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR distribution.

claim: 12 TLRs (TLR1–9, TLR11–13) have been identified in mice.
source: To date, 10 TLRs (TLR1–10) have been identified in humans and 12 (TLR1–9, TLR11–13) in mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR distribution.

claim: RIG-I like receptors (RLRs) include RIG-I, MDA5 and LGP2.
source: RLRs, which include RIG-I, MDA5 and LGP2, detect viral double-stranded RNA in the cytoplasm and activate a signaling cascade that leads to the production of type-I interferons and other antiviral molecules (Yoneyama and Fujita, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoneyama and Fujita, 2009.

claim: RLRs detect viral double-stranded RNA in the cytoplasm and activate a signaling cascade that leads to the production of type-I interferons and other antiviral molecules.
source: RLRs, which include RIG-I, MDA5 and LGP2, detect viral double-stranded RNA in the cytoplasm and activate a signaling cascade that leads to the production of type-I interferons and other antiviral molecules (Yoneyama and Fujita, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoneyama and Fujita, 2009.

claim: RNA from commensal bacteria can stimulate the RIG-I pathway.
source: Recently, we found that RNA from commensal bacteria could also stimulate the RIG-I pathway (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Mice lacking MAVS are highly sensitive to experimental colitis in part because of defective immune response to commensal bacterial RNA.
source: Mice lacking the mitochondrial protein MAVS (also known as IPS-1, VISA or CARDIF), which is an essential adaptor protein in the RLR pathway, are highly sensitive to experimental colitis in part because of defective immune response to commensal bacterial RNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: MAVS is an essential adaptor protein in the RLR pathway.
source: Mice lacking the mitochondrial protein MAVS (also known as IPS-1, VISA or CARDIF), which is an essential adaptor protein in the RLR pathway, are highly sensitive to experimental colitis in part because of defective immune response to commensal bacterial RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAVS function.

claim: IFNβ induction by commensal bacterial RNA depends on MAVS.
source: Interestingly, whereas IFNβ induction by commensal bacterial RNA depends on MAVS, the induction of proinflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β (IL-1β), depends on MyD88 (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: The induction of proinflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β (IL-1β), by commensal bacterial RNA depends on MyD88.
source: Interestingly, whereas IFNβ induction by commensal bacterial RNA depends on MAVS, the induction of proinflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β (IL-1β), depends on MyD88 (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Transfection of RNA from Lactobacillus salivarius (LAB) strongly induced IL-1β in mouse bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDM) and Raw264.7.
source: Our previous studies showed that transfection of RNA from Lactobacillus salivarius (LAB), a gram-positive commensal bacterium commonly found in the gastrointestinal tract, strongly induced IL-1β in mouse bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDM) and Raw264.7, a mouse macrophage cell line (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Lactobacillus salivarius is a gram-positive commensal bacterium commonly found in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Our previous studies showed that transfection of RNA from Lactobacillus salivarius (LAB), a gram-positive commensal bacterium commonly found in the gastrointestinal tract, strongly induced IL-1β in mouse bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDM) and Raw264.7, a mouse macrophage cell line (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Lactobacillus salivarius.

claim: LAB RNA added to the culture media of BMDM and Raw264.7 without transfection reagent strongly induced IL-1β.
source: Interestingly, even when LAB RNA was added to the culture media of BMDM and Raw264.7 without the transfection reagent FuGENE, it still strongly induced IL-1β (Figure 1A), which suggests that the RNA detection probably does not involve a cytoplasmic RNA sensor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The detection of LAB RNA probably does not involve a cytoplasmic RNA sensor.
source: Interestingly, even when LAB RNA was added to the culture media of BMDM and Raw264.7 without the transfection reagent FuGENE, it still strongly induced IL-1β (Figure 1A), which suggests that the RNA detection probably does not involve a cytoplasmic RNA sensor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that transfection is not required for IL-1β induction.

claim: RNase T1 but not RNase III destroyed the IL-1β inducing activity of LAB RNA.
source: RNase T1 but not RNase III destroyed the IL-1β inducing activity of LAB RNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNase V1 destroyed the IL-1β inducing activity of LAB RNA.
source: RNase V1, which digests both dsRNA and ssRNA at high concentrations, also destroyed the activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ssRNA from LAB is responsible for IL-1β induction.
source: Thus, ssRNA from LAB was responsible for IL-1β induction.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNase treatment experiments.

claim: IL-1β induction by LAB RNA was abolished in BMDM from MyD88−/− mice.
source: This induction was abolished in BMDM from MyD88−/− mice but not Mavs−/−, TLR2−/−TLR4−/−, or TLR7−/− mice (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: IL-1β induction by LAB RNA was not abolished in BMDM from Mavs−/−, TLR2−/−TLR4−/−, or TLR7−/− mice.
source: This induction was abolished in BMDM from MyD88−/− mice but not Mavs−/−, TLR2−/−TLR4−/−, or TLR7−/− mice (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Unc93b1 is essential for the trafficking of endosomal TLRs from the ER to the endosomal membrane.
source: To determine if the detection of LAB RNA occurs in the endosome, we used BMDM from the 3d mouse, which harbors a loss of function mutation in Unc93b1, a protein essential for the trafficking of endosomal TLRs from the ER to the endosomal membrane (Tabeta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tabeta et al., 2006.

claim: The induction of IL-1β by LAB RNA was abolished in 3d BMDM.
source: The induction of IL-1β by LAB RNA was abolished in the 3d BMDM (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: IL-1β induction by the TLR7 ligand R848 was dependent on Unc93b1.
source: As controls, IL-1β induction by the TLR7 ligand R848, but not the TLR4 ligand LPS, was dependent on Unc93b1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: IL-1β induction by the TLR4 ligand LPS was not dependent on Unc93b1.
source: As controls, IL-1β induction by the TLR7 ligand R848, but not the TLR4 ligand LPS, was dependent on Unc93b1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Members of the TLR11 family are localized on the endosomal membrane.
source: Previous studies have suggested that members of the TLR11 family are localized on the endosomal membrane (Brinkmann et al., 2007; Pifer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brinkmann et al., 2007 and Pifer et al., 2011.

claim: TLR11−/− BMDM induces IL-1β normally in response to LAB RNA.
source: TLR11−/− BMDM induces IL-1β normally in response to LAB RNA (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Knockdown of TLR13 significantly reduced IL-1β induction by LAB RNA.
source: The knockdown of TLR13 by both shRNA vectors significantly reduced IL-1β induction by LAB RNA, but not by the TLR7 ligand R848 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Knockdown of TLR13 did not reduce IL-1β induction by the TLR7 ligand R848.
source: The knockdown of TLR13 by both shRNA vectors significantly reduced IL-1β induction by LAB RNA, but not by the TLR7 ligand R848 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Expression of an RNAi-resistant TLR13 cDNA in the TLR13-shRNA cells rescued IL-1β induction by LAB RNA.
source: Importantly, expression of an RNAi-resistant TLR13 cDNA in the TLR13-shRNA cells rescued IL-1β induction by LAB RNA (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TLR13 is required for IL-1β induction by bacterial RNA.
source: These results indicate that TLR13 is required for IL-1β induction by the bacterial RNA.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: 23S rRNA, but not 16S or 5S rRNA, potently stimulated IL-1β production.
source: Strikingly, 23S, but not 16S or 5S, rRNA potently stimulated IL-1β production (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 23S rRNA from E. coli DH5α strongly induced IL-1β.
source: This activity was not limited to gram-positive bacterial RNA, because 23S rRNA from the E. coli strain DH5α, a gram-negative bacterium, also strongly induced IL-1β (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In vitro-transcribed 23S rRNA, but not 16S rRNA, induced IL-1β.
source: Remarkably, the in vitro-transcribed 23S, but not 16S, rRNA induced IL-1β, indicating that 23S rRNA contains unique sequences capable of activating the TLR13 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 23S rRNA contains unique sequences capable of activating the TLR13 pathway.
source: Remarkably, the in vitro-transcribed 23S, but not 16S, rRNA induced IL-1β, indicating that 23S rRNA contains unique sequences capable of activating the TLR13 pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro transcription experiments.

claim: A sequence located between nt 1894 and 2384 of 23S rRNA is important for IL-1β induction.
source: Deletion of 520 nucleotides (nt) from the 3′ end (nt 1–2384 based on E. coli sequence) did not impair the ability of the RNA to induce IL-1β, but further deletion of another 490 nt (1–1894) did, suggesting that a sequence located between nt 1894 and 2384 is important (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by deletion analysis shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The stimulatory RNA sequence is located at nt 2035–2074 of 23S rRNA.
source: Further deletion analysis narrowed down the stimulatory RNA sequence to nt 2035–2074 (Figure 4C–H), which was still fully capable of inducing IL-1β.
evidence: This is supported by deletion analysis shown in Figure 4C-H.

claim: The 15 nt RNA sequence (2054–2068), ACGGAAAGACCCCGU, is a strong inducer of IL-1β.
source: This analysis showed that the 15 nt RNA sequence (2054–2068), ACGGAAAGACCCCGU, was a strong inducer of IL-1β (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experiments using chemically synthesized RNA shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Deletion of one residue (A) from the 5′ end of the 15 nt sequence reduced the IL-1β stimulatory activity by about eightfold.
source: Further deletion of one residue (A) from the 5′ end reduced the IL-1β stimulatory activity by about eightfold (Figure 5B; compare 2054–2068 with 2055–2068), and deletion of another residue (C) from the 5′ end abolished the activity (2056–2068).
evidence: This is supported by deletion analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletion of another residue (C) from the 5′ end of the 14 nt sequence abolished the IL-1β stimulatory activity.
source: Further deletion of one residue (A) from the 5′ end reduced the IL-1β stimulatory activity by about eightfold (Figure 5B; compare 2054–2068 with 2055–2068), and deletion of another residue (C) from the 5′ end abolished the activity (2056–2068).
evidence: This is supported by deletion analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletion of two nucleotides (2054–2066) from the 3′ end was tolerable.
source: Deletion of two nucleotides (2054–2066) from the 3′ end was tolerable, but further deletion of another nucleotide (2054–2065) decreased the activity dramatically (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by deletion analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Further deletion of another nucleotide (2054–2065) from the 3′ end decreased the IL-1β stimulatory activity dramatically.
source: Deletion of two nucleotides (2054–2066) from the 3′ end was tolerable, but further deletion of another nucleotide (2054–2065) decreased the activity dramatically (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by deletion analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The optimal immune stimulatory RNA sequence resides in 2054–2066 of 23S rRNA (ACGGAAAGACCCC).
source: Titration experiments using varying concentrations of different RNA oligos suggest that the optimal immune stimulatory RNA sequence resides in 2054–2066 of 23S rRNA (ACGGAAAGACCCC) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by titration experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Point mutations at each residue from position 2055 to 2064 abolished the activity of the ISR23 RNA.
source: Point mutations at each residue from position 2055 to 2064 abolished the activity of the RNA, whereas an A>G mutation at position 2054 was tolerable (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: An A>G mutation at position 2054 of ISR23 was tolerable.
source: Point mutations at each residue from position 2055 to 2064 abolished the activity of the RNA, whereas an A>G mutation at position 2054 was tolerable (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A mutation of A at position 2058 to any of the other three nucleotides abolished the activity of ISR23.
source: Notably, a mutation of A at position 2058 to any of the other three nucleotides abolished the activity, but 2′-O-methylation of A at this position had no detrimental effect (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 2′-O-methylation of A at position 2058 had no detrimental effect on ISR23 activity.
source: Notably, a mutation of A at position 2058 to any of the other three nucleotides abolished the activity, but 2′-O-methylation of A at this position had no detrimental effect (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Point mutations at positions 2058, 2060 and 2061 in the full-length 23S rRNA abolished IL-1β induction.
source: We also introduced point mutations at positions 2058, 2060 and 2061 in the full-length 23S rRNA and found that each of these mutations abolished IL-1β induction (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The induction of IL-1β by both full-length 23S rRNA and nt 2054–2068 was markedly reduced by two distinct TLR13 shRNAs.
source: The induction of IL-1β by both full-length 23S rRNA and nt 2054–2068 was markedly reduced by two distinct TLR13 shRNAs, indicating that ISR23 also engaged TLR13 to induce IL-1β (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ISR23 engages TLR13 to induce IL-1β.
source: The induction of IL-1β by both full-length 23S rRNA and nt 2054–2068 was markedly reduced by two distinct TLR13 shRNAs, indicating that ISR23 also engaged TLR13 to induce IL-1β (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is inferred from the knockdown experiments.

claim: The ISR23 sequence is located in domain V of 23S rRNA, which is the catalytic center of the ribozyme responsible for peptide bond formation.
source: The ISR23 sequence is located in domain V of 23S rRNA, which is the catalytic center of the ribozyme responsible for peptide bond formation (Cech, 2000; Nissen et al., 2000) (Figure 5G; also see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cech, 2000 and Nissen et al., 2000.

claim: The ISR23 sequence is highly conserved among gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria, including E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes and LAB.
source: The ISR23 sequence is highly conserved among gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria, including E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes and LAB (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Haloarcula marismortui 23S rRNA contains 4 nucleotides that diverge from the conserved sequence of ISR23.
source: However, Haloarcula marismortui 23S rRNA, for which the crystal structure has been solved (Ban et al., 2000), contains 4 nucleotides that diverge from the conserved sequence of ISR23.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ban et al., 2000 and sequence comparison.

claim: The ISR23 variant sequence from H. marismortui failed to stimulate IL-1β.
source: Interestingly, this ISR23 variant sequence from H. marismortui failed to stimulate IL-1β (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Some bacteria might escape immune surveillance by TLR13 through mutations in the ISR23 sequence.
source: Thus, some bacteria might escape immune surveillance by TLR13 through mutations in the ISR23 sequence.
evidence: This is speculated based on the H. marismortui data.

claim: Stimulation of WT BMDC with the 23S rRNA sequence led to accumulation of pro-IL-1β, but not mature IL-1β.
source: Stimulation of WT BMDC with the 23S rRNA sequence led to accumulation of pro-IL-1β, but not mature IL-1β (Figure 6F, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: When WT BMDC were stimulated with the 23S rRNA sequence and then transfected with the DNA poly[dA:dT], mature IL-1β was detected.
source: When the cells were stimulated with the 23S rRNA sequence and then transfected with the DNA poly[dA:dT], which activates the AIM2 inflammasome (Schattgen and Fitzgerald, 2011), matured IL-1β was detected (lane 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Poly[dA:dT] activates the AIM2 inflammasome.
source: When the cells were stimulated with the 23S rRNA sequence and then transfected with the DNA poly[dA:dT], which activates the AIM2 inflammasome (Schattgen and Fitzgerald, 2011), matured IL-1β was detected (lane 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schattgen and Fitzgerald, 2011.

claim: Neither pro-IL-1β nor mature IL-1β was detected in Tlr13 KO cells stimulated by the 23S rRNA sequence.
source: Neither pro-IL-1β nor mature IL-1β was detected in Tlr13 KO cells stimulated by the 23S rRNA sequence (lanes 11 and 12).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: LPS and poly[dA:dT] treatment induced pro-IL-1β and mature IL-1β even in the absence of TLR13.
source: In contrast, LPS and poly[dA:dT] treatment induced pro-IL-1β and mature IL-1β even in the absence of TLR13 (lanes 9 and 10).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: TLR13 is essential for the induction of pro-IL-1β by bacterial ribosomal RNA.
source: These results indicated that TLR13 was essential for the induction of pro-IL-1β by bacterial ribosomal RNA but this receptor alone was insufficient to trigger inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoblot experiments.

claim: TLR13 alone is insufficient to trigger inflammasome activation.
source: These results indicated that TLR13 was essential for the induction of pro-IL-1β by bacterial ribosomal RNA but this receptor alone was insufficient to trigger inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoblot experiments.

claim: TLR13-deficient macrophages were completely defective in inducing IL6, IL10, TNFα and MCP1 in response to the 23S rRNA sequence.
source: TLR13-deficient macrophages were also completely defective in inducing other cytokines, including IL6, IL10, TNFα and MCP1, in response to the 23S rRNA sequence (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6G-J.

claim: G2061 is hydrogen bonded to A2451, the catalytic residue of peptide bond synthesis.
source: Notably, G2061 (based on E. coli sequence) is hydrogen bonded to A2451, the catalytic residue of peptide bond synthesis (Nissen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nissen et al., 2000.

claim: Both G2061 and A2451 are completely conserved in the large ribosomal RNA subunits of all three kingdoms.
source: Both G2061 and A2451 are completely conserved in the large ribosomal RNA subunits of all three kingdoms, suggesting a universal mechanism of peptide bond synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome conservation.

claim: The conservation of G2061 and A2451 suggests a universal mechanism of peptide bond synthesis.
source: Both G2061 and A2451 are completely conserved in the large ribosomal RNA subunits of all three kingdoms, suggesting a universal mechanism of peptide bond synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation data.

claim: C2063 forms a base pair with G2447.
source: Another residue of the ISR23 sequence, C2063, forms a base pair with G2447, which in turn forms a hydrogen bond with A2451 (Nissen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nissen et al., 2000.

claim: G2447 forms a hydrogen bond with A2451.
source: Another residue of the ISR23 sequence, C2063, forms a base pair with G2447, which in turn forms a hydrogen bond with A2451 (Nissen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nissen et al., 2000.

claim: The hydrogen bonding between G2447 and A2451 increases the pKa of A2451, allowing it to serve as a general base to catalyze peptide bond synthesis.
source: This hydrogen bonding increases the pKa of A2451, allowing it to serve as a general base to catalyze peptide bond synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome catalysis.

claim: TLR13 targets the most conserved and essential feature of bacteria, namely peptide bond formation.
source: Thus, TLR13 targets the most conserved and essential feature of bacteria, namely peptide bond formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the location of ISR23 in the catalytic center.

claim: The antibacterial mechanism of TLR13 is analogous to that of many antibiotics, which target the catalytic center of bacterial ribosomes.
source: This antibacterial mechanism of TLR13 is analogous to that of many antibiotics, which target the catalytic center of bacterial ribosomes (McCusker and Fujimori, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McCusker and Fujimori, 2012.

claim: Oldenburg et al. (2012) showed that the conserved 23S rRNA sequence 'CGGAAAGACC' is a ligand for TLR13.
source: Similar results have recently been published by Oldenburg et al. (2012), who showed that the conserved 23S rRNA sequence 'CGGAAAGACC' is a ligand for TLR13.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oldenburg et al., 2012.

claim: Oldenburg showed that N6 methylation at A2085 of S. aureus (corresponding to A2058 of E. coli 23S rRNA), which conferred antibiotic resistance, abolished TLR13 stimulation.
source: Interestingly, Oldenburg showed that N6 methylation at A2085 of S. aureus (corresponding to A2058 of E. coli 23S rRNA), which conferred antibiotic resistance, abolished TLR13 stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oldenburg et al., 2012.

claim: The extremely high degree of sequence specificity of TLR13 is unprecedented for nucleic acid sensing receptors.
source: The extremely high degree of sequence specificity of TLR13 is unprecedented for nucleic acid sensing receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other nucleic acid sensors.

claim: TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 detect RNA or DNA in the endosomal lumen without significant sequence specificity.
source: TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 detect RNA or DNA in the endosomal lumen without significant sequence specificity; instead, they recognize the structures of RNA or DNA (e.g., dsRNA for TLR3 and unmethylated CpG DNA for TLR9).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR function.

claim: TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 recognize the structures of RNA or DNA.
source: TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 detect RNA or DNA in the endosomal lumen without significant sequence specificity; instead, they recognize the structures of RNA or DNA (e.g., dsRNA for TLR3 and unmethylated CpG DNA for TLR9).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR function.

claim: RIG-I detects viral and bacterial RNA in the cytosol through the recognition of dsRNA bearing 5′-triphosphate.
source: RIG-I detects viral and bacterial RNA in the cytosol through the recognition of dsRNA bearing 5′-triphosphate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RIG-I function.

claim: MDA5 detects viral dsRNA and perhaps some other unknown features.
source: MDA5 detects viral dsRNA and perhaps some other unknown features.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MDA5 function.

claim: AIM2 binds dsDNA in the cytoplasm to trigger inflammasome activation.
source: AIM2 binds dsDNA in the cytoplasm to trigger inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AIM2 function.

claim: None of the cytosolic nucleic acid sensors display significant sequence specificity.
source: None of these cytosolic nucleic acid sensors display significant sequence specificity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cytosolic nucleic acid sensors.

claim: The high degree of RNA sequence specificity of TLR13 may allow rodents and other organisms that carry this gene to effectively combat some bacterial pathogens while minimizing potential autoimmune attacks to the host.
source: The high degree of RNA sequence specificity of TLR13 may allow rodents and other organisms that carry this gene to effectively combat some bacterial pathogens that threaten their survival while minimizing potential autoimmune attacks to the host.
evidence: This is speculated based on the sequence specificity data.

claim: Bacteria could mutate or modify residues in the ISR23 sequences to render the bacterium invisible to TLR13.
source: First, although bacteria cannot mutate the invariant residues in 23S rRNA that are important for peptide bond synthesis (e.g., G2061 and C2063), they could mutate or modify other residues in the ISR23 sequences to render the bacterium invisible to TLR13, as shown for H. marismortui (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is speculated based on the H. marismortui data.

claim: Two human mRNAs, which encode the ribosomal subunit S14 (RPS14) and a pancreatic lipase (PNLIP), have the exact sequence match to ISR23.
source: Although mammalian ribosomal RNAs do not have significant sequence homology to ISR23, we found by a BLAST search that two human mRNAs, which encode the ribosomal subunit S14 (RPS14) and a pancreatic lipase (PNLIP), respectively, have the exact sequence match to ISR23.
evidence: This is supported by BLAST search results.

claim: Total RNA from human cells do not trigger IL-1β production in murine macrophages.
source: Since total RNA from human cells do not trigger IL-1β production in murine macrophages (data not shown), the ISR23-like sequence in these mRNAs may be folded into secondary structures that cannot be detected by TLR13.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (not shown).

claim: The ISR23-like sequence in human RPS14 and PNLIP mRNAs may be folded into secondary structures that cannot be detected by TLR13.
source: Since total RNA from human cells do not trigger IL-1β production in murine macrophages (data not shown), the ISR23-like sequence in these mRNAs may be folded into secondary structures that cannot be detected by TLR13.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of IL-1β induction by human RNA.

claim: Unfolded RNA or fragments of human RPS14 and PNLIP mRNAs containing the ISR23 sequence could stimulate TLR13.
source: Nevertheless, it remains possible that unfolded RNA or fragments of these RNA (e.g., in dying or dead cells) containing the ISR23 sequence could stimulate TLR13.
evidence: This is speculated based on the sequence match.

claim: Humans might have abandoned TLR13 and relied on other pathogen receptors to detect pathogenic bacterial infections while avoiding autoimmune attacks.
source: Thus, human might have abandoned TLR13 and relied on other pathogen receptors including RLRs, NLRs and other TLRs to detect pathogenic bacterial infections while avoiding autoimmune attacks.
evidence: This is speculated based on the absence of TLR13 in humans.

claim: The loss of TLR13 in humans might have helped the expansion of the large commensal bacterial communities in the gut.
source: The loss of TLR13 in human might have also helped the expansion of the large commensal bacterial communities in the gut, which is important for the development of the immune system.
evidence: This is speculated based on the role of commensal bacteria.

claim: Humans lack the entire TLR11 subfamily, including TLR11, TLR12 and TLR13.
source: It is interesting to note that humans lack the entire TLR11 subfamily, including TLR11, TLR12 and TLR13 (Roach et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roach et al., 2005.

claim: TLR11 detects a profilin-like protein in Toxoplasma gondii and is important for the production of IL-12 in dendritic cells in mice.
source: TLR11 was shown to detect a profilin-like protein in Toxoplasma gondii and is important for the production of IL-12 in dendritic cells in mice (Yarovinsky et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yarovinsky et al., 2005.

claim: Humans have highly effective innate and adaptive immune responses against T. gondii despite lacking TLR11 protein.
source: Despite the lack of TLR11 protein (due to a stop codon in the coding sequence), humans have highly effective innate and adaptive immune responses against T. gondii.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human immunity to T. gondii.

claim: Humans might have evolved to abandon TLR11 to avoid autoimmune attacks and rely on other innate immune sensors to detect T. gondii infection.
source: As profilin is abundantly present in human cells, humans might have evolved to abandon TLR11 to avoid autoimmune attacks and rely on other innate immune sensors to detect the parasite infection (Balenga, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Balenga, 2007.

claim: TLR13 is essential for cytokine induction by the bacterial 23S rRNA.
source: Our data obtained from the TLR13 knockout macrophages show that TLR13 is essential for cytokine induction by the bacterial 23S rRNA, a phenotype that has not been observed with other TLR mutant mice, including those lacking TLR2, 4, 7 or 11.
evidence: This is supported by data from TLR13 knockout mice.

claim: The phenotype of TLR13 knockout has not been observed with other TLR mutant mice, including those lacking TLR2, 4, 7 or 11.
source: Our data obtained from the TLR13 knockout macrophages show that TLR13 is essential for cytokine induction by the bacterial 23S rRNA, a phenotype that has not been observed with other TLR mutant mice, including those lacking TLR2, 4, 7 or 11.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other TLR knockout mice.

claim: TLR13 may cooperate with other TLRs to detect bacterial infections.
source: However, this does not exclude the possibility that TLR13 may cooperate with other TLRs to detect bacterial infections.
evidence: This is speculated based on the complexity of bacterial infections.

claim: In the context of bacterial infections, multiple TLRs are likely to be activated by distinct ligands associated with bacteria.
source: In fact, in the context of bacterial infections, multiple TLRs are likely to be activated by distinct ligands associated with bacteria, including peptidoglycans, flagellin, lipopolysaccharides, DNA and RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of bacterial components and TLR ligands.

claim: TLR13 might take up bacterial RNA on the cell surface and traffic to the endosome where it launches the signaling cascades.
source: Our finding that the ISR23 RNA could stimulate mouse macrophages without transfection suggests that TLR13 might take up bacterial RNA (i.e., from dead or lysed bacteria) on the cell surface and traffic to the endosome where it launches the signaling cascades.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that transfection is not required.

claim: The TLR13 signaling cascade engages MyD88 and Unc93b1.
source: The TLR13 signaling cascade clearly engage MyD88 and Unc93b1, but the details of the signaling pathway requires further dissection.
evidence: This is supported by data from MyD88 and Unc93b1 knockout/mutant mice.

claim: ISR23 may not be an adjuvant for the development of human vaccines.
source: Finally, although ISR23 may not be an adjuvant for the development of human vaccines, its potent activity in stimulating cytokine production may be employed to boost the production of antibodies in vertebrate animals that possess the TLR13 pathway.
evidence: This is speculated based on the absence of TLR13 in humans.

claim: ISR23's potent activity in stimulating cytokine production may be employed to boost the production of antibodies in vertebrate animals that possess the TLR13 pathway.
source: Finally, although ISR23 may not be an adjuvant for the development of human vaccines, its potent activity in stimulating cytokine production may be employed to boost the production of antibodies in vertebrate animals that possess the TLR13 pathway.
evidence: This is speculated based on the potent cytokine-inducing activity of ISR23.
